summary.text: Legendre’s formula, together with a floor-function inequality sharpened using the congruence \(8n\equiv 2r+1\pmod{p^i}\), shows that each factor \(8n-(2r+1)\) divides \((8r+3)!\,a(n)\); prime powers already present in \((8r+3)!\) cover the remaining cases. Inductively adjoining the factors then works because their gcd with the preceding product is uniformly bounded: each pairwise gcd divides the difference \(2(r-k)\), so the total overlap divides \(((2r)!)^r\).

full_proof.text: Let \[ X_n=(8n)!\,n!,\qquad Y_n=(4n)!(3n)!(2n)!, \] so that the sequence in the statement is \[ a(n)=\frac{X_n}{Y_n}. \] We will first prove that this quotient is an integer. We then prove a uniform divisibility statement for each individual factor \(8n-(2r+1)\), and finally combine the individual factors by induction. Throughout, \(v_p(N)\) denotes the exponent of a prime \(p\) in a positive integer \(N\). We use Legendre's formula \[ v_p(M!)=\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lfloor\frac{M}{p^i}\right\rfloor. \] All the sums which occur here have only finitely many nonzero terms. ## 1. A basic floor inequality and the integrality of \(a(n)\) We first establish that, for all positive integers \(P\) and all nonnegative integers \(n\), \[ \left\lfloor\frac{4n}{P}\right\rfloor+ \left\lfloor\frac{3n}{P}\right\rfloor+ \left\lfloor\frac{2n}{P}\right\rfloor \leq \left\lfloor\frac{8n}{P}\right\rfloor+ \left\lfloor\frac{n}{P}\right\rfloor. \tag{1} \] Write \(n=qP+t\), where \(0\leq t8r+3 \tag{4} \] and \[ 8n=(2m+1)P+2r+1 \tag{5} \] for some nonnegative integer \(m\). Then \[ \left\lfloor\frac{4n}{P}\right\rfloor+ \left\lfloor\frac{3n}{P}\right\rfloor+ \left\lfloor\frac{2n}{P}\right\rfloor+1 \leq \left\lfloor\frac{8n}{P}\right\rfloor+ \left\lfloor\frac{n}{P}\right\rfloor. \tag{6} \] To prove this, put \[ n=qP+s,\qquad 0\leq s4u-1, \] and, since all quantities are integers, this implies \[ P\geq4u. \tag{7} \] From (5), and from \(00. \] We claim that \[ dY_n\mid X_nH_r. \tag{15} \] Once this is proved, (3) turns (15) into \[ dY_n\mid a(n)H_rY_n. \] Since \(Y_n>0\), cancellation gives \(d\mid a(n)H_r\), which is (14). It remains to prove (15). Fix a prime \(p\), and write \[ v=v_p(d),\qquad h=v_p(H_r). \] By Legendre's formula, the desired valuation inequality \[ v_p(d)+v_p(Y_n)\leq v_p(X_n)+v_p(H_r) \tag{16} \] is obtained by summing, over \(i\geq1\), the termwise inequalities \[ \begin{aligned} &\left\lfloor\frac{4n}{p^i}\right\rfloor+ \left\lfloor\frac{3n}{p^i}\right\rfloor+ \left\lfloor\frac{2n}{p^i}\right\rfloor +\mathbf 1_{i\leq v}\\ &\hspace{25mm}\leq \left\lfloor\frac{8n}{p^i}\right\rfloor+ \left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor +\mathbf 1_{i\leq h}, \end{aligned} \tag{17} \] where \(\mathbf 1_E\) is \(1\) if \(E\) holds and \(0\) otherwise. Indeed, \[ \sum_{i\geq1}\mathbf 1_{i\leq v}=v, \qquad \sum_{i\geq1}\mathbf 1_{i\leq h}=h. \] Put \(P=p^i\). The basic floor inequality (1) proves (17) immediately unless \[ i\leq v\quad\text{and}\quad i>h. \tag{18} \] If both indicators are equal, or if the left indicator is zero, no strengthening is needed. Thus only (18) requires attention. Under (18), \(P=p^i\mid d\). Also \[ P>8r+3. \tag{19} \] Indeed, if \(P\leq8r+3\), then \(P\) is one of the positive integers not exceeding \(8r+3\), so \(P\mid(8r+3)!=H_r\). Since \(P=p^i\), this would imply \(i\leq v_p(H_r)=h\), contrary to (18). The integer \(d=8n-(2r+1)\) is odd. Since \(p^i\mid d\), both \(p\) and \(P=p^i\) are odd. Write \[ d=cP. \] The quotient \(c\) is also odd, so \(c=2m+1\) for some \(m\geq0\). Thus \[ 8n=(2m+1)P+2r+1. \] Together with (19), these are precisely the hypotheses of the strengthened floor inequality (6). Therefore \[ \left\lfloor\frac{4n}{P}\right\rfloor+ \left\lfloor\frac{3n}{P}\right\rfloor+ \left\lfloor\frac{2n}{P}\right\rfloor+1 \leq \left\lfloor\frac{8n}{P}\right\rfloor+ \left\lfloor\frac{n}{P}\right\rfloor. \] In the exceptional situation (18), the left indicator in (17) is \(1\) and the right indicator is \(0\), so this is exactly (17). Hence (17) holds for every \(i\geq1\). Summing it proves (16) for every prime \(p\), and therefore proves (15). The proof of the one-factor statement (14) is complete. ## 4. A uniform bound for the gcd created when a new factor is adjoined For \(r,n\geq0\), define \[ D_r(n)=\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}\bigl(8n-(2j+1)\bigr), \tag{20} \] with the empty product \(D_0(n)=1\). When passing from \(r\) to \(r+1\), the new factor is \[ B_r(n)=8n-(2r+1), \] and \[ D_{r+1}(n)=D_r(n)B_r(n). \tag{21} \] We need a bound, depending on \(r\) but not on \(n\), for \(\gcd(D_r(n),B_r(n))\).
